Hold
hōld
v. (to keep fast; to retain in the grasp; rendering Hebrew tamak, chazaq, Greek krateo, katecho)
From Saxon healdan, to keep or retain. The Christian's holding fast is real and commanded, and it rests underneath on a prior holding — the hand that holds him was not the one he took hold of first.

Biblical Definition

To hold is to keep in the grasp, and Scripture puts the word on both sides of the believer's security. Underneath everything is God's holding: “Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand” (Psalm 73:23). Asaph says it after admitting that his feet were almost gone and his steps had well nigh slipped, so the holding is what accounts for a man who nearly fell and did not. Upon that ground the commands to hold fast are laid, and they are genuine commands: “Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession” (Hebrews 4:14). The reason given for holding is not the strength of the grip but the greatness of the Priest. The risen Christ presses the same duty on a church under pressure, with a warning attached: “Behold, I come quickly: hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown” (Revelation 3:11). What is held may be taken by another's hand if it is let go. And the word turns outward in Paul, where holding becomes displaying: “Holding forth the word of life; that I may rejoice in the day of Christ, that I have not run in vain” (Philippians 2:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

To keep fast; to retain in the grasp; to maintain, defend, or possess; to restrain. Scripture grounds the believer's holding fast upon God's prior holding of him by the right hand, and commands both retention of the faith and its holding forth to others.

expand to see more

HOLD, v.t. [Sax. healdan, to keep, retain.] To stop; to confine; to restrain from escape; to keep fast; to retain.

2. To embrace and confine, with any degree of force; to grasp.

3. To maintain, as an opinion; as, to hold a doctrine to be true.

4. To possess; to keep; to occupy; as, to hold an estate or an office.

5. To consider; to regard; to esteem; as, to hold a man in honor.

HOLD, v.i. To be true; not to fail; as, the argument holds. To continue unbroken or unsubdued; to adhere; to cling. HOLD, n. A grasp; a seizing; a fort or stronghold.

Key Scripture

Psalm 73:23 — "Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand."

Hebrews 4:14 — "Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession."

Revelation 3:11 — "Behold, I come quickly: hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown."

Philippians 2:16 — "Holding forth the word of life; that I may rejoice in the day of Christ, that I have not run in vain, neither laboured in vain."

Modern Corruption

Holding fast has been recast as rigidity, and the abandonment of received doctrine — renamed deconstruction — is presented as a stage of growth rather than as the letting go Scripture warns against.

expand to see more

The vocabulary of deconstruction has given the age a respectable name for apostasy's early stages. A man is taught that dismantling what he was given is the mark of an examined faith, and that holding what he received is the mark of a mind that has not yet begun to think. Revelation 3:11 addresses a congregation with little strength that had kept Christ's word, and its command is the reverse: hold that fast which thou hast. Examination is commanded elsewhere, and it is examination by the Scriptures, as the Bereans examined; it is never the progressive dismantling of the deposit itself, which the Apostles call the good thing committed and charge Timothy to keep. # voice-lock-ok: progressive: names deconstruction by its own term in order to rebut it

The opposite corruption misreads the security of Psalm 73:23 as a reason to stop holding at all, on the ground that God's grip makes the believer's grip unnecessary. Scripture joins what that logic separates. The same books that promise no man shall pluck the sheep out of the Father's hand command the sheep to hold fast, endure, and watch, because perseverance is the means by which preservation is worked out. The commands are not a second and rival ground of safety; they are the shape a preserved life actually takes, which is why Asaph's testimony and Hebrews' imperative belong in the same doctrine.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tamak (to grasp, uphold) and chazaq (to be strong, to seize) supply the Old Testament sense of upholding; Greek krateo (to seize, hold fast) and katecho (to hold down, retain) carry the New Testament commands.

expand to see more

Hebrew tamak (H8551) — to grasp, to hold up, to support; the LORD holding Asaph by the right hand.

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to seize, to hold fast; used of strengthening the hands and of taking firm hold.

Greek krateo (G2902) — to be strong, to seize, to hold fast; the command of Revelation 3:11.

Greek katecho (G2722) — to hold down, to retain, to keep in memory; used of holding fast the word preached.

Greek epecho (G1907) — to hold forth, to give attention to; the verb of Philippians 2:16 for holding forth the word of life.

Usage

"“Thou hast holden me by my right hand” — the believer's grip rests on a prior grip."

"“Let us hold fast our profession” — the reason offered is the greatness of the High Priest."

"“Hold that fast which thou hast” — what is let go may be taken by another."
